title: Seven frameworks, no attack: how often the alarms fire
dek: MAST-Data holds {runs_in_file} runs of seven agent frameworks doing ordinary tasks. None is an attack. The Alert rule fired in {alert} of the {runs} we could read.
kicker: MAST-Data, a public dataset of agent-team runs

source.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
source.attribution: Excerpts are from MAST-Data (MAD): Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2503.13657; data at huggingface.co/datasets/mcemri/MAST-Data, licensed CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Changes: each run's log text was split into turns by our reader, and each excerpt is cut short.
source.input: the AppWorld and HyperAgent runs, as logged (python3 -I agenttrace/failure_eval.py story seven-frameworks-no-attack)

body.p: The audit of this project asked for real benign traffic from teams of agents. MAST-Data has it: [[c1|{runs_in_file} runs of seven agent frameworks]] on ordinary tasks such as writing a small program or answering a question. Each run comes with a mark for each of fourteen kinds of task failure. [[c2|The marks were made by a language-model judge, not by people]], so we use them only as a rough split between runs that failed and runs that did not.

Each framework logs in its own layout, as one block of text. Our reader keeps the agent turns and leaves the other log lines out. [[c3|{timed} of the {records} records carry a time the framework printed]]. The rest have only their order.

None of these runs is an attack. [[c4|The Alert rule fired in {alert} of {runs}]]. It asks for two kinds of coordination sign, and a team that takes turns in one conversation shows two within its first few messages. [[c5|The Watch rule fired in {watch}]]: words such as token, secret and delete are ordinary in programming work. [[c6|The hourly volume baseline fired in {volume}]], and that says nothing, because it needs half a day of history and a run lasts minutes.
A real clock does not change this. [[c7|In ChatDev, which prints its times, the Alert rule fired in {cd_alert} of {cd_runs} runs]].

Three of the frameworks name the recipient of a message in the log. [[c8|{logged} messages are addressed]]. With the recipients removed, [[c9|the tool found {pair_found} of the {pair_logged} sender-recipient pairs]] from speaking order alone. [[c10|In one run a supervisor asks a music agent a question]], and the tool links the two because the agent speaks next. It cannot tell which of several instructions an answer belongs to: [[c11|in ChatDev it found {cd_msg} of {cd_logged} single messages]].

[[c12|The Watch rule fired on {watch_failed} of the runs marked as failed and {watch_clean} of the clean ones]]. Most of that gap is the mix of frameworks. [[c13|{ag_clean} of the {clean} clean runs come from one framework]], and there the rule almost never fires on any run. The rules were written for attacks. Nothing here shows that they see task failure.

body.note: Credit for the data and the marks is in the source line below and beside each excerpt.

docs.label: MAST-Data in the dataset registry: source, licence, what the tool can and cannot do with it

c1.caveat: Data: Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., "Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?", NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2503.13657, huggingface.co/datasets/mcemri/MAST-Data, CC BY 4.0. We changed the form, not the words: each run's log was split into turns.

docs.label: The dataset card, which says the annotations come from an LLM judge

c3.caveat: ChatDev, MetaGPT and OpenManus print times. The other four frameworks do not; their runs are placed on a step clock, sixty seconds a record, which keeps the order and invents nothing else.

c4.evidence: The Alert rule on benign runs.
c4.caveat: Counted once per run. The intervals and the table for each framework are in reports/external/mast_data/summary.md.

c5.evidence: The Watch rule on benign runs.

c6.caveat: A zero here is not a result. The baseline compares an hour with the hours before it, and no run is long enough.

c7.evidence: The same rule on a framework with logged times.

c8.evidence: Messages whose recipient the log names (ChatDev, AppWorld, HyperAgent).

c9.evidence: Pairs found with the recipients removed.
c9.caveat: A pair is a sender and a recipient inside one run. Pairs in one run are not independent, so an interval over pairs would be too narrow.

c10.evidence: One addressed message and the turn after it.

records.note: The log's header for this turn is "Message to spotify Agent", inside the supervisor's call: sender and recipient are both written down.
The agent's next turn. With recipients withheld, this is what the tool links to the supervisor.

c10.caveat: Excerpts from MAST-Data (Cemri, Pan, Yang et al., NeurIPS 2025; CC BY 4.0), split into turns by our reader and cut short.

c11.evidence: Single messages found with the recipients removed.
c11.caveat: The tool counts each write once per reader. In a long two-way chat it has the pair after the first exchange and adds little after that.

c12.evidence: The Watch rule against the judge's marks.

c13.evidence: Where the clean runs come from.
c13.caveat: Inside one framework the gap is small or absent, and most frameworks have too few clean runs to say. The table is in reports/external/mast_data/summary.md.
